title: Build AI Agents to Automate Your Workflows
purpose: Instructor-led O’Reilly template companion with trial onboarding, editable teaching diagrams, cited notes, and universal decision exercises.

slides.title:
Build AI Agents
to Automate
Your Workflows
lines: Microsoft Copilot Studio
Tim Warner | September 8, 2026
slides.notes: Hello there, and welcome to Build AI Agents to Automate Your Workflows. Tim Warner here, and over the next four hours I'm gonna teach you to build a Copilot Studio agent that earns its keep. We're building the Contoso AI Fundamentals Coach, an agent that helps a colleague prepare for Azure AI Fundamentals, which is exam AI-901. We'll grow that same agent all morning. First it gets a clear job, then a trusted source, then a conversation that actually waits for an answer, then a bounded tool, and finally a pilot decision you can defend. The exam is just our subject matter. The design skill transfers straight to your help desk, your onboarding, and your internal knowledge work, and you won't write a line of code to get there.

slides.title: The four course outcomes
lines: Plan a Copilot Studio agent from persona, job-to-be-done, instructions, topic map, guardrails, and success metrics.
Build a grounded AZ-900 study assistant using knowledge sources, topics, generative answers, and test prompts.
Extend the agent with actions, agent flows, MCP and subagent concepts, and human handoff patterns.
Evaluate, publish, observe, and govern the agent using analytics, agent evaluations, Power Platform Well-Architected guidance, and security principles.
slides.notes: These four outcomes are what you signed up for, so let's be straight about how we'll hit them. I'll build one agent across four segments and show you the evidence behind every change, not just the happy-path chat. You don't need a tenant to take part, because every exercise is a prediction, a diagnosis, or a design decision you can make on paper. One housekeeping note on outcome two: it says AZ-900 because that's the wording approved before AI-900 retired this past June. AI-901 replaced it under the same certification name, so AI-901 is what we're building. Same skill, current exam. If your account's ready, follow along, and the full recipes are in the repo for later.

slides.title: A maker and a learner
lines: You: design the assistant
Contoso colleague: learn Azure AI
Shared need: useful practice with a source
slides.notes: Contoso's a fictional company and this is a fictional enablement program, so nothing here is a real customer. Our user has twenty or thirty minutes to study and keeps tripping over unfamiliar AI concepts. You're the maker, which means the quality of that experience sits with you. The agent explains one narrow concept, asks an original practice question, waits for the answer, and then gives feedback. It can hand back a reviewed study session. It can't book an exam, it doesn't know anyone's personal calendar, and it won't promise a passing score. Hold onto that last part, because most of today's interesting decisions sit right on that boundary.

slides.title: The agent’s building blocks
lines: User message through a channel
Generative orchestration
Knowledge: reference material
Topic: authored conversation
Tool: a defined operation
slides.notes: Read this diagram from the user's message toward the capabilities. A channel carries the conversation in, and a trigger starts the work. With generative orchestration turned on, the agent reads your descriptions and picks what to use: knowledge, topics, tools, or several at once. Knowledge contributes reference material, topics hold the dialogue you authored, and tools run a defined operation. Instructions steer behavior, but here's the part people skip past: instructions don't grant data access and they don't guarantee a correct answer. A conversational trigger and an event trigger are different front doors, and today we're using the conversational one. Treat this as a conceptual map, not a guaranteed execution order.

slides.title: Starting a Copilot Studio trial
lines: Open the official Copilot Studio trial sign-up
Enter a work or school email address
Follow the account-specific sign-up prompts
Open the available authoring environment
slides.notes: Let me show you the official trial route, straight from the current Get access article on Microsoft Learn. You enter a work or school email, select Next, and follow whatever prompts that account gets. Now I won't pretend there's one universal screen sequence here, because tenant configuration and existing entitlement change what appears. I'm using an instructor-controlled account for this, and you can watch the whole route without creating anything today. And if the account's already licensed, I'll say so and explain what we're actually looking at rather than dressing it up as a fresh trial. That kind of honesty about your own demo environment is worth more than a polished lie.

slides.title: Trial access and its limits
lines: What happens | What to do
Work or school identity is required | Use the appropriate organizational account.
Self-service signup is blocked | Use the documented administrator route.
Trial authoring and testing are available | Practice with synthetic course data.
Publishing is unavailable on the trial | Watch the entitled instructor publish demo.
rows: Work or school identity is required
Trial authoring and testing are available
Publishing is unavailable on the trial
Watch the entitled instructor publish demo.
slides.notes: Here's the honest shape of trial access. You can author and you can test, but you can't publish. A personal email address or an organizational self-service restriction can stop sign-up cold, and the fix is the documented administrator route, not a policy you change on the fly during a class. Watch the two expiry clocks as well, because the trial license and the trial environment aren't the same thing. Read the actual notices in your own tenant instead of trusting a sixty-day number you half-remember. Save your work through the documented process before anything expires. Nothing today depends on you finishing sign-up.

slides.title: The brief before the build
lines: Brief element | Contoso example
Persona and job | An AI beginner needs supported explanations and practice.
Instructions | Use the course reference. Say when it doesn’t support an answer.
Boundary | No exam booking, private policy claims, or pass guarantees.
Success metric | Zero invented policy answers in the recorded boundary test set.
slides.notes: Read the persona and the job together, because a brief you can't test is just a wish. Ask yourself what evidence would separate a genuinely helpful answer from a confident invention, and write that down as your metric. Ours is zero invented policy answers across the boundary cases we actually run. Notice the hedge in that sentence, because it covers the cases we run and it isn't a guarantee about every future response. Save the brief before you open a single authoring control. A small topic and tool inventory pays you back later, because when something odd happens you can tell which capability got selected.
rows: A cloud beginner needs supported explanations and practice.
Use the course reference. State when it does not support an answer.

slides.title: One map, five purposes
lines: Purpose | Course implementation
Overview | Grounded explanation from the course reference
Practice | One authored teach-question-feedback topic
Study plan | GetStudySession flow
Fallback | Honest limitation and mentor referral
Search | Knowledge retrieval with source inspection
slides.notes: A purpose on your topic map doesn't automatically need its own authored topic, and that's worth internalizing early. Overview and search can both ride on grounded answers. Practice is different, because we need the agent to stop and wait for new thinking from the learner, and that takes a controlled dialogue. Study planning goes to the tool we build in segment three. Fallback explains what the agent couldn't do and offers a next step that's actually true. We'll author the practice sequence explicitly and inspect the fallback path. Write descriptions that genuinely distinguish these purposes, because that's exactly what orchestration reads when it chooses.
rows: Grounded explanation from the course reference

slides.title: The shell and the first boundary
lines: Demo: blank agent, instructions, orchestration
Test: “What is my exact exam appointment?”
Your decision: one topic, one instruction, one metric
slides.notes: Now we're cooking with gas. I'll create a blank agent in the documented standard experience, check the orchestration setting and the approved model, and save the instructions. Then I'll run the exam appointment prompt in a fresh conversation. Watch what happens, because the source can't know a personal fact like that, and this is our first honest boundary test. Inspect the response rather than assuming the instruction did its job. That's the habit I want you carrying out of this room. While I demo, you write one instruction, one topic purpose, and one metric. No account needed, and we aren't spending this whole segment on sign-up screens.

slides.title: 10-minute break
lines: Return at 10:00 AM Central
Build: the source and the conversation
slides.notes: Take the scheduled ten minutes. The teaching clock stops here.

slides.title: The source behind an answer
lines: Question
Retrieve relevant passage
Generate an answer
Inspect answer and source
slides.notes: Grounding means the agent pulls evidence from a reference at response time instead of leaning on whatever the model already absorbed. We'll use the small Contoso AI concepts file so we can inspect a source we actually know. That file's course-authored teaching material grounded in Microsoft Learn, and it isn't a Microsoft publication or a complete exam syllabus. I'll ask which responsible AI principle covers telling somebody they're talking to a bot, then compare the generated answer against the passage behind it. A citation's something you inspect, not an accuracy certificate. We'll test the unsupported appointment question separately. This diagram explains retrieval conceptually, and it isn't a promise that every answer takes this path.

slides.title: Knowledge scope and limits
lines: Choice | Consequence for this assistant
Agent knowledge | A shared reference for general study questions
Topic grounding | A selected source scope for a particular conversation
Source order | No “first uploaded source wins” rule
Limits and citations | Check source readiness, scope, and the supporting passage
slides.notes: Agent-level knowledge is available broadly across the conversation. A generative answers node can narrow to a selected source scope, and you'll want to inspect its Search only selected sources setting rather than guessing at it. Don't teach upload order as source priority, because there's no first-uploaded-wins rule in there. Names and descriptions are what drive selection. For this controlled build I'm turning off broad web search and ungrounded responses, and then testing. Those settings have limits and they don't guarantee every claim is correct. The guide records current size and source-count limits with the docs. One small text file is a teaching choice that keeps setup quick, not a product ceiling.
rows: A shared reference for general study questions
A selected source scope for a particular conversation
Check source readiness, scope, and the supporting passage

slides.title: Teach, wait, then give feedback
lines: Message: teach the concept
Question: WAIT for a choice
Correct choice: explain why
Incorrect choice: explain misconception
Unmatched twice: offer recovery
slides.notes: Here's a trap worth naming out loud. A question mark inside a Message node doesn't make the agent wait for anything at all. You need a Question node with real multiple-choice options and a saved response variable. Set it to ask every time, because a practice answer has to come from the learner right now, not from something they said earlier in the conversation. The correct branch and the incorrect branches should explain genuinely different things. An unmatched answer needs an honest recovery. I'll test the first turn to prove the answer key stays hidden, then reply to check the feedback.

slides.title: Context reuse or a new answer?
lines: Situation | Use
“Give me a responsible-ai study session” | Dynamically fill the tool/topic input from context
Assistant asks: “Which principle covers transparency?” | Question node; wait for the learner’s choice
A required value is missing | Prompt for it; do not guess
An answer doesn’t match | One reprompt, then a truthful recovery
slides.notes: Automatic input filling earns its place when the conversation already tells us which focus the learner wants. It's the wrong tool for collecting a fresh quiz answer, and that distinction matters more than it looks. The proposal uses the term AutomaticTaskInput. What's documented in the authoring experience today is Dynamically fill with the best option, with a separate Should prompt user control. So we'll teach the documented controls, and I won't claim the proposal term is a current interface label or invent YAML for it. I'll show you the difference on a tool input and on a Question node, then get back to the build.

slides.title: The practice topic, built together
lines: Watch: lesson → Question node → feedback
Predict the next turn before I run it
Identify the wait point and explain one wrong-answer branch
slides.notes: I'll author and test the practice topic while you predict what it does. Before I run the first test, ask yourself whether the assistant should reveal the answer at that point, and hold your answer. Use the seven-minute exercise from the Build guide, sketch or annotate the node sequence, and write the feedback you'd give for one wrong choice. No tenant account required. Then we'll watch the actual wait, the actual feedback, and the recovery on an unmatched answer, and compare all of that against what you predicted. The full lab's there for independent practice later, and designing on paper isn't the same as authoring it.

slides.title: A useful failure response
lines: Unsupported: “I don’t have your exam appointment.”
Recovery: “Check your booking confirmation.”
Human boundary: “I can’t contact a mentor from here.”
slides.notes: A good failure response names what's missing and gives a next step that genuinely exists. We'll inspect both the authored topic's recovery and the system fallback route, because instructions alone won't change a system fallback message. And a topic named Escalate doesn't prove a single human was contacted. Use the fallback and escalation guidance so you don't promise a transfer you can't deliver. Then we'll debrief what we saw: the source passage, the wait point, the branch-specific feedback, and the limitation. Ask yourself which of those you'd have missed if you'd only watched a polished final chat transcript.

slides.title: 10-minute break
lines: Return at 11:00 AM Central
Extend: one useful tool
slides.notes: Take the scheduled ten minutes. The teaching clock stops here.

slides.title: The next action
lines: User request | Appropriate next step
Explain a responsible AI principle | Answer using knowledge
Give me a study session; focus unspecified | Clarify the focus
Give me the responsible-ai study session | Call GetStudySession
Book my exam or decide an accommodation | Refer to an authorized human or service
slides.notes: The right next step depends entirely on the job in front of the agent. Use these four requests to separate generating a supported answer from collecting information and from running an operation. Our tool returns a fixed, reviewed session, which gives us an unambiguous capability boundary to look at, and it doesn't write to any external system. Now ask yourself why a booking request belongs outside this agent's authority, because that's the real lesson on this slide. I'd rather keep the tool demo focused on input, execution, and evidence than bolt on a connector just to make the thing look impressive.
rows: Give me a study session; focus unspecified
Give me the cloud study session
Book my exam or decide an accommodation
Refer to an authorized human or service

slides.title: GetStudySession: the contract
lines: Input: focus
GetStudySession native agent flow
Outputs: status and plan, both Text
slides.notes: The input's one Text value: responsible-ai, workloads, or foundry. Those are Contoso teaching shortcuts, and I want to be precise here, because they aren't the official AI-901 skill area names. The outputs are status and plan, both Text. A supported focus returns ok plus a reviewed thirty-minute session. An unsupported value like quantum returns unsupported and a reminder of the choices. A runtime failure's a different animal from an unsupported value, and we'll test those separately. The flow never books, mails, or updates a record. This becomes a real tool pattern once the flow's built and bound, because the fixture on its own isn't a deployed flow.

slides.title: The flow behind the tool
lines: Agent calls flow
Initialize status and plan
If responsible-ai
If workloads
If foundry
Respond once
slides.notes: Let's get the vocabulary straight, because this trips people up constantly. The tool is the capability the agent can call. The agent flow implements that capability, and the designer's actions are steps inside it. Follow the native recipe: when an agent calls the flow, initialize String variables for status and plan at the top level, evaluate three conditions, and respond exactly once after the branches. Keep the default unsupported response unless a supported focus matches. That native response is synchronous, so it has to meet the documented timeout. We don't need loops, arrays, or a hosted API to teach this first boundary.

slides.title: The evidence of a tool call
lines: Expected input: focus = responsible-ai
Expected output: status = ok; plan describes 30 minutes
No execution record? The response alone is insufficient.
slides.notes: This is my favorite few minutes of the whole morning. I'll run the direct flow test first, then request the responsible-ai session through the agent. Then we inspect the actual input and the returned status and plan in the activity view. Count the allocation with me: ten minutes reading, ten minutes working an example, five minutes recalling without notes, and five minutes checking against Microsoft Learn. We'll test unsupported input and tool unavailability as two separate conditions. These slide values describe the expected contract, and they aren't results we observed while writing the course. If I play a rehearsal recording, I'll tell you it's a recording first.

slides.title: HTTP and MCP
lines: Mechanism | What the maker needs to understand
HTTP tool | A defined endpoint, request contract, and response
MCP server | Available capabilities, their descriptions, and server access
Both | Identity, permitted data, errors, and approval
This workshop | One native agent flow; other mechanisms are comparisons
slides.notes: An HTTP tool calls one defined web operation. Model Context Protocol gives you a way to expose discoverable tools and resources through a server, and the reviewed Copilot Studio integration for it requires generative orchestration. Neither mechanism grants permission just by being connected, and that's the sentence I'd underline twice. For Contoso, a future approved learning catalog might expose one web operation, or a server with several described tools. We aren't building either integration in this first tool lesson. What you need to explain is which boundary each one introduces and which identity does the calling. Keep authentication, endpoint restrictions, and data policy inside that decision.

rows: A defined endpoint, request contract, and response

slides.title: When another agent helps
lines: Parent agent
Child agent: specialized work
Connected agent: separately managed
A2A: a protocol for agent communication
slides.notes: Now you might be thinking, hang on Tim, everybody's shipping multi-agent systems right now, so why are we staying with one? Because you add specialization when another agent has a genuinely distinct job or a different owner, not because multi-agent sounds impressive on a slide. A child agent's organized inside a parent. A connected agent can be managed separately. Agent-to-agent describes an interoperability protocol rather than a third ownership model. Current Microsoft guidance also lists connections involving Microsoft Foundry, Fabric, and the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK, and their prerequisites differ. Those are extension awareness today, not working course integrations. So what new responsibility would justify a second agent?

slides.title: Authority and human handoff
lines: Claim | Evidence required
“Contact your mentor” | A truthful route the user can take
“I submitted your request” | A real authorized operation and returned receipt
“You are connected to a person” | A supported handoff and accepted transfer
“The tool can access this data” | The intended identity and policy allow that access
slides.notes: Don't confuse a friendly sentence with a completed business operation. That's the whole slide, honestly. A referral tells the user where to go. Submitting a request requires a real authorized connector and a returned receipt proving it went through. A live transfer requires a supported integration and an accepted handoff on the other end. Our course agent only offers a mentor referral, and it says so plainly. The same logic applies to authentication, because instructions can't grant permissions. Check the execution identity, the connector policy, and the allowed data before you add a tool or an external model, and use synthetic content for the exercise.

A real authorized operation and returned receipt
A supported handoff and accepted transfer

slides.title: Your tool decision
lines: For Contoso: name the input and expected output
Distinguish an unsupported focus from an unavailable tool
Name one request that needs a human
slides.notes: Three minutes, everybody, on the same Contoso contract. No account and no flow attachment needed. Give me the input, the two output fields, and one request the tool should refuse as unsupported. Then I'll use the prepared agent and flow to inspect real execution evidence, and we'll revisit the failures together. Keep your predictions labeled as predictions until we've actually observed something, because that discipline is most of what separates a working agent from a demo that fooled everybody. The independent tool lab stays available after class for anyone who wants to build it themselves.

slides.title: Two evaluation sets, two questions
lines: Prepared set | Question it answers

AI901-live-three
Compare meaning: E04, E05, E08 | Does the response match the expected meaning?

AI901-tool-one
Tool use: E08 only | Did it use the actual GetStudySession capability?
Separate manual conversation | Did the topic wait, then give the correct feedback?
slides.notes: We start from prepared native sets so we spend our time interpreting results instead of typing test cases. AI901-live-three uses Compare meaning across E04, E05, and E08, each with an expected response. AI901-tool-one uses Tool use only for E08 and selects the actual GetStudySession capability. Remove the default General quality method when you're building deliberately focused sets like these. Methods get configured on the set, so leaving expected tools blank on the other two cases produces Invalid results for that method rather than a clean skip. The eighty-percent meaning threshold's our course choice, not a Microsoft recommendation. And single-response grading never simulates answering the quiz.

slides.title: A score and an execution trace
lines: Same test set
Run before
One change
Run after
Compare individual cases
Inspect source and tool trace
slides.notes: Run the same prepared set before your change and after it. One change, not five. Open a failed case, read the expected response against the actual one, then inspect the activity map for the knowledge passage or the tool call behind it. A generated grading rationale can be wrong, so verify the underlying evidence rather than trusting the score on its face. Compare the same set, not different questions that happen to produce a friendlier number. If you change the agent model, record the approved configuration and rerun the same cases. Export genuine results with the documented control, and never pass authored expectations off as an executed report.

slides.title: Usage signals need interpretation
lines: Signal | What it does and doesn’t tell us
10 sessions: 9 did not escalate | 90% containment proxy
6 resolved; 3 abandoned; 1 escalated | 60% resolution; 30% abandonment
4 survey responses | The survey describes those 4 respondents
High containment and wrong answers | Inspect outcomes, transcripts, and source evidence together
slides.notes: Everything on this slide is synthetic discussion data rather than tenant telemetry, and I'll say that again before we leave it. In the guide's ten-session example, nine sessions didn't escalate, but only six actually resolved. Three were abandoned and one escalated. So a ninety-percent containment proxy sits right next to a sixty-percent resolution rate, and that gap is the entire lesson. The survey describes its four respondents, not your user base. Test-panel traffic's excluded from Monitor, and channel data can arrive late. Read resolution, abandonment, transcripts, feedback, and response time together, because any one of them alone will mislead you.

slides.title: Five Well-Architected concerns
lines: Concern | Control for the study assistant
Reliability | Tool failure has a clear recovery path.
Security | Use the intended identity and approved sources.
Operational Excellence | An owner reviews repeatable tests and incidents.
Performance Efficiency | Measure response time and unnecessary tool work.
Experience Optimization | Wait for the learner; give useful feedback and a next step.
slides.notes: Use the Power Platform framework as a thinking tool rather than reciting five labels back at people. Reliability means a useful recovery when the tool's unavailable. Security means an approved identity and permitted data. Operational excellence means repeatable tests and an owner who can actually respond when something breaks. Performance efficiency means measuring response time and unnecessary tool work instead of assuming a longer answer's a better one. Experience optimization means the learner gets useful feedback, understands the limitation, and can reach a real next step. These are course examples of the framework applied, not a Microsoft certification of our agent.

slides.title: Publishing and audience access
lines: Tested draft
Publish configured version
Scoped channel and access
Fresh session with actual user
slides.notes: Publishing makes the configured version available to connected channels. It doesn't by itself establish who can use the thing, and that distinction catches people out constantly. I'll use an entitled instructor environment, a prepared scoped Teams channel, and a fresh conversation, then run one publish operation and two short checks, with the second-user access check prepared separately. I won't ask trial-only learners to publish, because current licensing guidance permits creation and testing but not publication. Environment separation, data policy, and an approved audience all belong in rollout planning. An installation link isn't evidence that anyone was actually granted access.

slides.title: Channel choice changes the checks
lines: Channel | Preparation to verify
Teams: course demonstration | Entitlement, scoped access, installation, fresh conversation
SharePoint: comparison | Site permission, published agent, allowed deployment
Microsoft 365 Copilot: comparison | Channel configuration and approved audience
Every channel | Actual user access, source permissions, and behavior
slides.notes: Teams is our live channel today. SharePoint and Microsoft 365 Copilot are scoped comparisons, and each route carries its own setup, permissions, and availability. For SharePoint the maker needs the documented site access and deployment prerequisites. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, inspect the channel configuration and the approved audience rather than assuming your Teams setup lights up every surface. Test the fresh conversation behavior with the actual intended user. And here's a hard line from me: never use a public channel as a workaround for a private pilot that got blocked. That isn't a shortcut, that's a governance incident waiting to happen.

slides.title: Your pilot decision
lines: Name one agent worth piloting
Choose its users, owner, data boundary, and stop condition
Cite one result and label its evidence source
slides.notes: Protect seven minutes for the Operate worksheet. A good candidate might be a small internal enablement pilot with approved content and a named owner. I want you to name what would stop the pilot, not just what would start it, because that's the part everybody skips. Use the synthetic case if you don't have real observations, and label the evidence for exactly what it is. A worksheet's evidence of your reasoning, and it isn't evidence that publishing or evaluation executed. Then I'd like one of you to challenge somebody else's pilot boundary using the five concerns.

slides.title: The same pattern at work
lines: Course component | Workplace transfer
AI-901 reference | Approved internal knowledge
Practice topic | A controlled training or triage interaction
Study-session tool | One bounded lookup or operation
Pilot decision | Named audience, owner, evidence, and stop condition
slides.notes: Transfer the architecture, not the exam subject. A help-desk agent could ground in approved support articles, use a topic for triage, and call one approved lookup. An onboarding assistant could ground in approved guidance and refer a sensitive case to a person. Every new scenario needs its own access review and its own evaluation cases. For follow-up, inspect a genuine topic capture in the native code editor or in VS Code. That YAML represents authored structure, and it isn't a magic portable deployment. The export guide walks the procedure, and the sanitized capture has to come from the teaching tenant before anybody distributes it.

slides.title: The four outcomes in practice
lines: Plan: a brief with a testable boundary
Build: source evidence and a topic that waits
Extend: a tool contract and a human boundary
Operate: test evidence and a defensible pilot decision
slides.notes: Let's bring it home with the four outcomes. You planned a brief with a testable boundary. You grounded answers in a real source and built a topic that genuinely waits. You gave the agent a bounded tool and drew a human boundary around it. And you produced test evidence plus a pilot decision you can defend in a room full of stakeholders. Your brief, your prediction, your tool decision, and your pilot decision are real artifacts even without a tenant. A blocked operation stays unrun, and a prediction never counts as a passing test. I hope you found this session helpful, and I'll see you next time.
